newsitem.title: PERU: INTERVIEW - Lima bolsa president sees trouble ahead.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Lima bolsa president sees trouble ahead.

text.p: The President of the Lima Stock Exchange, Jose Luque Otero, warned that growing political turmoil in Peru could jeopardize investor confidence and the nation's future development.

"I believe everything possible is being done to make this country considered high-risk for investors," Luque Otero told Reuters late Tuesday. "That is not fair, because Peruvians have paid dearly to get out of the hole."
The market suffered its biggest loss of the year on Tuesday when the bolsa's general index .IGRA slid 5.64 percent and the blue-chip index .ISEL fell by the same figure.

The political panorama heated up over the weekend when TV station Frecuencia Latina aired a program showing proof that the country's secret services had been bugging the phones of politicians, journalists, industrialists and artists.

The situation worsened when officials revoked the nationality of the owner of Frecuencia Latina, Israeli-born Baruch Ivcher, who was granted citizenship in 1984 by ex- president Fernando Belaunde. The government said the measure was taken because of "administrative irregularities" in Ivcher's immigration forms.

Amid the outrage over these developments, President Alberto Fujimori's approval rating hit a new low. A survey issued Wednesday by leading pollster Apoyo put Fujimori's popularity at 23 percent -- the lowest in seven years of power and a fall of 11 percent in just nine days.

"This sequence of events makes it impossible to predict what will happen tomorrow," explained Luque Otero. "The phone espionage and the threats against the owner of a private enterprise is a violation of the established norms."
Luque Otero believes that if the current political problems affecting the bolsa were eliminated, it would be one of the most profitable in Latin America.

"In the middle of this critical moment we cannot calculate profitability for the rest of the year," he said. "However if the problems relaxed, (profitability) could be above 30 percent until the end of 1997."
Luque Otero believed many factors were responsible for Tuesday's stock market falll, but that the strongest was the political malaise.
"Many sold for profit-taking, and the whole region suffered from the devaluation of the Brazilian currency," he said. "However undoubtedly the political crisis had the biggest impact."
The fall marks the definitive end of a remarkable first half, when the bolsa rose 50.8 percent, led mostly by the polymetallic sector which benefited from rising zinc prices.
Also of interest was the banking sector, which after some reforms and merges, appeared very competent and profitable to investors.
Luque Otero said it was necessary "now more than ever" for Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori to take measures to solve the crises started by his officials.
"I urge the government to think about the country, for the good that we have obtained, for the future," he added.
